points.t: A child with a smooth, yellow-orange, hairless plaque on the scalp, or an adult with a warty plaque there.
A hamartoma of epidermis, hair follicles and sebaceous glands (mosaic HRAS/KRAS mutations); hormones thicken it at puberty.
Recognise, photograph and monitor; discuss elective excision; refer any new nodule, ulcer or bleeding within it.
A new lump or crusted area within the naevus (trichoblastoma, rarely BCC); extensive lesions with eye, brain or bone involvement (syndromic).

points: **Post-zygotic (mosaic) HRAS (most) or KRAS mutations.** This is why it follows Blaschko's lines and why the same mutation underlies the syndromic forms.
Well-demarcated, hairless, yellow-orange or pink plaque, usually oval on the scalp or linear on the face/neck child; skin of colour).
In adults: rough, warty, sometimes with papules or nodules inside it.
Clinical in most cases. Dermoscopy shows yellow globules and a cerebriform/papillomatous pattern.
Biopsy any **new nodule, ulcer, bleeding or rapid change** within a sebaceous naevus.
An extensive or facial lesion with neurological, ocular or skeletal signs needs paediatric referral for syndrome work-up.

cards.name: Aplasia cutis congenita
cards.clue: Membranous or scarred, atrophic, sometimes a "hair collar"; not yellow or waxy

cards.name: Epidermal (verrucous) naevus
cards.clue: Warty, brown, not yellow; often off the scalp

cards.name: Juvenile xanthogranuloma
cards.clue: Dome-shaped orange papule, not a plaque

cards.name: Linear morphoea en coup de sabre (see Other lumps and syndromes)
cards.clue: Acquired (not congenital), indurated, ivory, with hair loss and a groove; **progressive**

cards.name: Alopecia areata / tinea capitis
cards.clue: Acquired, with normal skin texture or scale

items.t: A new lump, crust, ulcer or bleeding within a sebaceous naevus: refer for **biopsy**.

pearls.t: Parents often worry about "cancer". Give the honest figures (secondary tumours are mostly benign, BCC under 1%) and teach them to look for **any lump growing within the patch**.
Teenagers notice the change at puberty. Reassure them it is expected, not malignant.
